label: Philosophy
title: Why We Can't Sit Alone in a Room – Pascal and the Art of Diversion
thumbnail_text: They chose the shock over silence
description: In the 17th century, Blaise Pascal wrote that all of humanity's unhappiness comes from one thing: we cannot stay quietly in a room. In 2014, a study in Science seemed to prove him right – many participants preferred giving themselves a mild electric shock to sitting alone with their thoughts. In this calm video essay we look at Pascal's Pensées, his idea of diversion (divertissement), the experiments by Timothy Wilson and his colleagues, and how we might learn to be at home in our own minds.

sections.text:
A small, plain room. No phone, no book, nothing to write with. Just a chair, and you, and your thoughts, for fifteen minutes.

On the table there is a button. If you press it, you get a mild electric shock. Earlier, you said you would pay money to avoid that shock.

Would you press it anyway?

In 2014, researchers ran almost exactly this experiment. A surprising number of people did press the button. And a French philosopher had predicted something like it more than three hundred years earlier.

sections.heading: A Note Left Unfinished

quote.lead: Blaise Pascal was a mathematician, inventor and religious thinker who lived from 1623 to 1662. He died before he could finish the book he was working on. His notes were published after his death as the Pensées, the Thoughts. One of them begins like this:
quote.text: I have discovered that all the unhappiness of men arises from one single fact, that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber.
quote.author: Blaise Pascal, Pensées 139 (Brunschvicg)

sections.text:
It is a bold claim. All the unhappiness of men, from one single fact.

Pascal arrived at it by watching people. He looked at the courtiers and soldiers of his time, at the quarrels, the passions and the risky ventures they threw themselves into. And he asked a simple question: why do people go to so much trouble?

A man with enough money to live, he observed, would not leave his home to go to sea or lay siege to a fortress, if only he knew how to stay at home with pleasure. The restlessness itself was the clue. Something in us does not want to be still.

Notice that Pascal does not say people are lazy, or that they lack discipline. He says something stranger. Even when nothing forces us to move, we choose to. We invent tasks, rivalries and worries, because being still feels harder than being busy.

sections.heading: The Chase, Not the Hare
sections.text:
Pascal had a word for what we do instead of sitting still: divertissement. Diversion. It means more than entertainment. It is anything that turns our attention away from ourselves.

His favourite example is the hunt. Offer a hunter a hare as a gift, and he will not want it. Yet he will spend a whole day chasing one through the fields. Why? Because it was never really about the hare. It was about the chase, the noise, the distraction.

The same goes, Pascal says, for games, for conversation, for ambition, for work. Even a king, surrounded by every pleasure, becomes unhappy the moment he is left alone with nothing to do. That is why kings are kept so busy, and surrounded by people whose job is to distract them.

And what are we fleeing from? For Pascal, the answer was our own condition. When we sit quietly, we begin to think about who we are, how fragile we are, and that we will die. Diversion, he thought, is how we avoid looking at that.

Pascal was a Christian, and his own answer to this restlessness was faith. But his description of the problem has spoken to readers of every belief, and of none.

sections.heading: Just Think
sections.text:
In 2014, the psychologist Timothy Wilson and his colleagues published a series of studies in the journal Science, under the title Just Think.

In the early studies, participants were left alone in a sparse room for somewhere between six and fifteen minutes, with no phone and nothing to read. Their only task was to entertain themselves with their own thoughts. Most people found it hard. Many reported that their minds wandered, and that they did not enjoy it much. When some participants did the same task at home, the results were similar, and a number of them admitted to cheating, checking a phone or getting up.

Then came the study that made the headlines. Participants first received a mild electric shock and rated how unpleasant it was. Many said they would pay to avoid it. Then they were left alone for fifteen minutes, with the option to shock themselves if they wanted to.

Two thirds of the men, and about a quarter of the women, pressed the button at least once. One man pressed it 190 times.

It is worth being careful here. The groups were small, and a shock you control is not the same as real suffering. Still, the result was striking enough to be discussed far beyond psychology.

The researchers did not conclude that people enjoy pain. Their interpretation was more modest, and more unsettling: for many of us, doing something, even something unpleasant, can feel easier than doing nothing at all.

sections.heading: Our Endless Chase
sections.text:
Pascal never saw a smartphone. But it is hard to read him today without thinking of one.

The moments of stillness that used to fill a day, waiting for a bus, standing in a queue, lying awake before sleep, can now be filled instantly. There is always another message, another video, another headline. The hare has become endless, and the chase never has to stop.

And the pull is not only towards screens. Many of us fill silence with plans, lists and small worries, rehearsing tomorrow instead of resting in today. The mind, too, can be a busy court.

None of these things are bad in themselves. Pascal did not think hunting or games were wicked. His point was about what they are for. If every quiet moment must be filled, it may be worth asking what we would meet in the silence, and why we are so keen to avoid it.

sections.heading: Learning to Sit
sections.text:
The good news from the research is that sitting with your thoughts seems to be partly a skill.

In later work, Erin Westgate, Timothy Wilson and Daniel Gilbert found that people often struggle not because thinking is unpleasant, but because they do not know what to think about. When participants chose a pleasant topic in advance, a memory, a plan, a place they love, the time alone became easier.

So you might try this. Once a day, put the phone in another room for ten minutes. Sit somewhere comfortable. Before you begin, choose something to think about, and let your mind wander from there.

The first few times, it may feel restless, even uncomfortable. That is normal. You are not doing it wrong. You are simply noticing the pull that Pascal described.

And if difficult thoughts come, you do not have to solve them. You can just let them be there for a while, and let them pass.

sections.heading: A Quiet Room
sections.text:
Pascal's claim was dramatic. Perhaps not all of human unhappiness comes from this single fact. But a surprising amount of our restlessness might.

Still, his question is worth carrying with us: what would happen if, just for a few minutes, we stopped running?

The room was never the problem. The room is just a room. What makes it hard is that, in the quiet, we finally meet ourselves.

Maybe that meeting does not have to be frightening. Maybe, with a little practice, it can become one of the calmest places we know.

short.title: They chose a shock over sitting alone
short.hook: Shock yourself or sit in silence?
short.text:
In 2014, researchers left people alone in a plain room for fifteen minutes. No phone. No book. Just their thoughts, and a button that gave them a mild electric shock.

Many had said they would pay to avoid that shock. Yet two thirds of the men and about a quarter of the women pressed the button at least once.

More than three hundred years earlier, Blaise Pascal wrote that all the unhappiness of men arises from one single fact: they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber.

Maybe the room was never the problem. In the quiet, we finally meet ourselves.
